**You are entitled to 12 days of paid annual leave for each year of service once you have worked for your employer for 3 years.**

**What the law says:**
Under (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(1)(b)), an employee is entitled to "twelve days for every twelve months of continuous service" (working for the same employer without a real break) when employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years. This leave is in addition to rest days and paid public holidays (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(1a)).

**What could change this:**
* **Better contract terms:** Your contract of service (employment agreement) can give you more leave, but any term giving less than the statutory minimum is void (Employment Act 1955, s.7).
* **Location:** The Act applies in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)). Sabah and Sarawak are governed by separate Labour Ordinances.
* **Unpaid leave:** Unpaid leave that exceeds 30 days in a 12-month period is disregarded when counting your length of service (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(3b)).
* **Unapproved absences:** If you miss more than 10% of working days without permission and without reasonable excuse, you lose your leave entitlement for that 12-month period (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(1)).

For consequential matters, verify the current statutory text at lom.agc.gov.my.

**Your employer must give you the notice written in your contract, or between 4 and 8 weeks of written notice based on your length of service.**

### What the law says
Under the law (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)), the notice period must be the same for both employer and employee. If your written contract does not set a period, the minimum notice is:
- 4 weeks if you have worked there for less than 2 years;
- 6 weeks if you have worked there for 2 years or more but less than 5 years;
- 8 weeks if you have worked there for 5 years or more.

The notice must be in writing (Employment Act 1955, s.12(4)).

### What could change this
- **Your contract:** A written contract can agree on a specific notice period (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
- **Payment in place of notice:** Either party may terminate immediately by paying an indemnity (compensation equal to wages for the notice period) (Employment Act 1955, s.13(1)).
- **Misconduct:** An employer may dismiss an employee without notice for misconduct after a due inquiry (a formal internal investigation or hearing) (Employment Act 1955, s.14(1)).
- **Location:** The Employment Act 1955 covers Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)). Sabah and Sarawak are governed by separate Labour Ordinances not covered here.

*Note: This snapshot may not reflect subsequent amendments; check the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**You are entitled to at least 98 consecutive days of maternity leave for each birth.**

**What the law says**
Under the law, an eligible female employee is entitled to maternity leave of *"not less than ninety-eight consecutive days"* for each confinement [giving birth after at least 22 weeks of pregnancy] (Employment Act 1955, s.37(1)(a)(i), s.37(1)(d)(ii), s.2(1)). 

**What could change this**
* **Paid vs unpaid leave:** You only get paid maternity allowance [wages during leave] if you worked for your employer for at least 90 days in the 9 months before giving birth, and worked at any time in the 4 months before giving birth (Employment Act 1955, s.37(2)(a)).
* **Number of surviving children:** You do not get maternity allowance if you already have 5 or more surviving children at the time of birth, though you still get the leave (Employment Act 1955, s.37(1)(c)).
* **Where you work:** The Employment Act 1955 applies in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)). Sabah and Sarawak have separate Labour Ordinances not covered here.
* **Your employment contract:** Your contract may provide more leave, but it cannot offer less.

To verify the current text, check lom.agc.gov.my.

**If you do not need a hospital stay, you get 14 to 22 days of paid sick leave each calendar year depending on your length of service. If you need hospital care, you get up to 60 days in total each calendar year.**

### What the law says
Under the Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1), after an examination at the employer's expense, your non-hospital sick leave entitlement per calendar year is:
- 14 days if you have worked there for less than 2 years (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(aa)(i)).
- 18 days if you have worked there for 2 years or more but less than 5 years (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(aa)(ii)).
- 22 days if you have worked there for 5 years or more (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(aa)(iii)).

If hospitalization is needed, you get "sixty days in the aggregate [total] in each calendar year" (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(bb)).

### What could change this
- **Location:** This Act applies only in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)); Sabah and Sarawak have separate labour ordinances not covered here.
- **Medical certification:** Leave must be certified by an approved registered medical practitioner [licensed doctor], medical officer, or dental surgeon (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1), s.60F(1a)).
- **Notice:** You must inform or try to inform your employer within 48 hours of your sick leave starting (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(2)(b)).
- **Overlapping leave:** You cannot take paid sick leave while receiving maternity allowance or temporary disability compensation (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(4)).

*(Note: Federal Acts are consolidated snapshots. Verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.)*

**Your employer cannot force you to retire before you turn 60 years old.**

**What the law says:**
The minimum retirement age is 60 years old (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.4(1)). An employer must not prematurely retire an employee before this age (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.5(1)), and any employment term setting a lower retirement age is void (legally invalid) (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.7(1)).

**What could change this:**
- **You choose to leave early:** You may still take optional retirement (retiring earlier by your own choice) if your contract allows it (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.6).
- **Excluded jobs:** This protection does not cover public sector employees, non-citizens, domestic servants, apprentices, probationers, part-time workers working under 70% of normal full-time hours, or certain fixed-term contracts (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.2(1) and Schedule).
- **Other reasons for termination:** An employer may still dismiss you for reasons unrelated to age, such as poor performance or misconduct (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.5(3)).

*(Note: These are consolidated snapshot Acts. Please verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.)*

**A trade union gets recognised by serving a formal written claim on an employer, who has 21 days to accept or give written reasons for refusing. If the employer refuses or does not reply, the union can report the matter to the Director General for Industrial Relations to investigate and decide.**

### What the law says
A trade union of workmen (an association of employees) begins the process by serving a claim for recognition on an employer in writing using the prescribed form (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(2)). 

Within 21 days, the employer must either accord recognition (formally agree to deal with the union) or notify the union in writing with grounds for refusal (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(3)). If the employer refuses or fails to respond, the union has 14 days to report the matter to the Director General (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4)). 

The Director General may check union membership scope or hold a secret ballot (a confidential vote among workers) to measure support, and issue a binding decision on whether recognition is granted (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4A), s.9(5)).

### What could change this
* **Job capacity**: A general union cannot seek recognition for workers employed in a managerial, executive, confidential, or security capacity (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(1)).
* **Missed deadlines**: If the union does not report an employer's refusal or silence within 14 days, the claim is treated as withdrawn (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4)).
* **Existing recognition**: If another union is already recognised for the same workers, no new claim can be made until 1 year has passed (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.11).

*Note: Federal Acts are updated periodically. You can verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Yes, anyone who lends money as a business in Malaysia must hold a valid moneylender's licence.**

**What the law says**
Under (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.5(1)), no person may carry on or advertise a business of moneylending (lending money at interest to a borrower) *"unless he is licensed under this Act"*. Operating without a licence is an offence carrying a fine between RM250,000 and RM1,000,000, imprisonment for up to 5 years, or both, plus possible whipping for repeat offences (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.5(2)).

**What could change this**
* **Statutory exemptions**: The Act does not apply to bodies listed in the First Schedule (such as licensed banks and pawnbrokers), which follow their own separate laws (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2A(1)).
* **Ministerial exemptions**: The Minister may specifically exempt certain companies or societies from the Act (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2A(2)).
* **Nature of the lending**: An isolated or personal loan made outside of a moneylending business may not fall under the licensing requirement (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2).

*Note: This summary is based on federal principal Acts. Please verify the latest law at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Generally no, a company cannot process your personal data without your consent, but there are specific legal exceptions where consent is not required.**

**What the law says**
Under the Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.6(1)(a), a data user (a person or business that controls or processes personal data) must not process personal data about a data subject (the individual the data is about) unless that person "has given his consent to the processing".

Even so, under the Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.6(2), a company may process your personal data without consent if it is necessary:
- to carry out a contract you are party to, or to take steps at your request before entering a contract;
- to comply with any legal obligation placed on the company by law (other than a contract);
- to protect your vital interests (matters relating to life, health, or safety);
- for the administration of justice; or
- to exercise powers or duties under any law.

**What could change this**
- **Type of transaction:** The Act only applies to personal data processed in commercial transactions (buying, selling, or exchanging goods and services) (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.2(1)).
- **Government agencies:** Federal and State Governments are completely exempt from this Act (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.3(1)).
- **Specific statutory exemptions:** Consent is not needed if the data is processed for investigating or preventing crime, complying with court orders, preparing statistics, or discharging certain regulatory functions (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.45).

*(Note: Malaysian federal statutes are consolidated snapshots. Verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.)*

**A company director must always act in good faith for the company's best interests, use reasonable care and skill, and avoid using company property or opportunities for personal gain.**

**What the law says:**
- Directors must exercise their powers "for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company" (Companies Act 2016, s.213(1)).
- Directors must exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence (careful and competent attention), based on standard expectations for that role and any extra skills they actually hold (Companies Act 2016, s.213(2)).
- Directors cannot use company property, internal information, position, business opportunities, or competing businesses for personal gain without approval at a general meeting (a meeting of company shareholders) (Companies Act 2016, s.218(1)).
- A nominee director (a director appointed to represent a specific member or employer) must never put that nominator's interests ahead of the company (Companies Act 2016, s.217(1)).

**What could change this:**
- Directors meet their care and diligence duties under the business judgment rule if they act in good faith, hold no personal interest, stay informed, and believe the decision is in the company's best interest (Companies Act 2016, s.214(1)).
- Directors may reasonably rely on reports from experts, officers, or fellow directors, or delegate tasks (Companies Act 2016, s.215, s.216).
- The company's constitution (its internal governing rulebook) can modify board management powers (Companies Act 2016, s.211(2)).

*(This covers federal Acts only, not case law. Check lom.agc.gov.my for the latest text.)*

**Compensation is based primarily on the market value of your land at the time the formal acquisition notice is published in the Gazette (the official government publication), plus qualifying moving costs or damage to your remaining property.**

What the law says:
The Land Administrator must determine compensation by considering only the statutory factors "and no others" (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 2):
- The market value (fair commercial price between a willing buyer and seller) assessed at the gazette notification or declaration date (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 1(1)).
- Damage caused by severing (splitting) the acquired portion from your other land, or injurious affection (harm caused to your other property) (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 2(c), (d)).
- Reasonable expenses if you are forced to move your home or place of business (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 2(e)).
- The award cannot exceed the amount you claimed during the inquiry (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 4(a)).
- The Land Administrator cannot consider your reluctance to part with the land or the urgency of the acquisition (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 3(a), (b)).

What could change this:
- Which state the land is in (this federal Act applies to Peninsular Malaysia; Sabah and Sarawak are governed by state land enactments).
- Whether only a portion is acquired, which may involve deductions if the project increases your remaining land's value (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 2(b)).
- Title restrictions, lease expiry dates, or special statuses like Malay reservation land (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, para 1(1D), (2), (2A)).

Federal principal Acts do not include court precedents or state land rules; verify current texts at lom.agc.gov.my.

**I couldn't find that in the Acts I have access to, because the exact minimum wage rate is set by subsidiary legislation (a Ministerial order published in the Gazette) rather than the principal Act.**

**What the law says**
Under the National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, the Minister makes a minimum wages order by notification in the Gazette following recommendations from the Council (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.23(1)). If your contract of service (an employment agreement) offers basic wages lower than that order, your rate must be *"substituted with any rates not lower than the minimum wages rates as specified in the minimum wages order"* (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.24(2)).

**What could change this**
* The specific minimum wage amount is set in subsidiary legislation (such as a Minimum Wages Order), which is not included in this corpus of federal principal Acts.
* The order may set different rates, starting dates, or exemptions depending on the sector, region, or type of employment (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.22(1)).

Please check lom.agc.gov.my to verify the latest subsidiary legislation and current statutory orders.

**Your employer must pay monthly contributions into your EPF based on the statutory rates set for your monthly wage band. Your employer must pay both its own share and your share up front, and cannot deduct its own share from your wages.** 

### What the law says
An employer is responsible in the first instance for paying both its own contribution and the employee's contribution for each month's wages (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.45(1), s.45(2)). The specific monthly sums are fixed by wage brackets set out in the Third Schedule (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.43(3), Third Schedule). The law also provides that an employer cannot "deduct or otherwise recover from the wages or remuneration of the employee, the employer’s contribution" (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.47(1)).

### What could change this
- **Your monthly wages**: The exact ringgit contribution depends on your monthly wage bracket (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, Third Schedule).
- **Your age**: Lower contribution rates apply once you reach 60 years of age (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, Third Schedule, Part C, Part D).
- **Citizenship status**: Different contribution rates apply to Malaysian citizens, permanent residents, and non-citizens (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, Third Schedule, Part C, Part D).
- **Voluntary higher rate**: Either you or your employer may elect (formally choose) to contribute at a higher rate (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.43(3)).
- **Approved funds**: EPF contributions are not payable if you are covered by an approved fund (a recognized alternative pension or provident scheme) (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.52(1)).

*Note: This text reflects the principal Act snapshot. Later amendments and subsidiary orders may change the active percentage rates; verify current rates at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Yes, you are generally covered by SOCSO if you are injured while travelling on a direct route to or from your place of work.**

**What the law says**
Under (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.24(1)–(2)), an accident that occurs while travelling between your residence and workplace is treated as an employment injury (a work-related personal injury). However, it is not covered if the accident happens during any *"interruption of, or deviation from, the insured person’s journey"* for personal reasons.

**What could change this**
* **Detours or interruptions:** If you take an unauthorized break or detour from your usual route for personal reasons, you are not covered.
* **SOCSO registration status:** You must qualify as an insured person (an employee for whom SOCSO contributions are payable). Certain casual workers and exempt categories are excluded (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.3(3), First Schedule).
* **Self-employed status:** If you work for yourself rather than under an employment contract, coverage is governed separately (Self-Employment Social Security Act 2017, s.3).

*This text reflects federal principal Acts; verify the latest amendments at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**I couldn't find that in the Acts I have access to. Islamic family matters in Selangor are governed by Selangor state enactments, not Malaysian federal legislation.**

**Why this is not in the database**
This corpus contains only Malaysian federal principal Acts. Under Malaysia's legal system, Syariah law and Islamic family matters fall under the jurisdiction of each individual state, which passes its own state enactments (such as the Islamic Family Law (State of Selangor) Enactment). 

This database does not contain state enactments, state Syariah laws, subsidiary legislation, or case law. To find the specific grounds for divorce in Selangor, you must refer to the relevant Selangor state enactment and state Syariah court rules.

**Stamp duty applies to written legal documents (instruments) listed in the First Schedule to the Stamp Act 1949, such as contracts, property transfers, loan documents, charges, leases, and deeds.**

**What the law says**
An instrument (Stamp Act 1949, s.2) "includes every written document". A document is chargeable with stamp duty if it falls under any description listed in the First Schedule (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule), including:
- Written contracts and agreements (Item 4)
- Conveyances (documents transferring ownership of property or shares) (Item 32)
- Charges or mortgages (documents giving a lender legal rights over property to secure a debt) and loan agreements (Items 22 and 27)
- Leases or tenancy agreements for immovable property (Item 49)
- Letters of guarantee and letters of allotment (Items 50 and 51)
- Deeds and declarations of trust (Items 37 and 38)

**What could change this**
- Certain documents are expressly exempt, such as service or employment agreements where monthly wages do not exceed RM300 (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule, Item 4).
- Instruments executed by or in favour of the Federal Government or State Rulers are generally exempt (Stamp Act 1949, General Exemptions).
- Whether the document was executed in Malaysia or brought into Malaysia after being executed overseas (Stamp Act 1949, s.42(1)).

*Note: Federal statutes are subject to amendments; verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**The exact stamp duty depends on your annual rent and the length of your tenancy, because the law uses a rate formula rather than a single fixed amount.**

### What the law says
If the total rent for the year is RM2,400 or less, the duty is zero (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule, item 49(a)(i)). 

For rent above RM2,400 per year, stamp duty is charged "for every RM250 or part thereof in excess of RM2,400" at these rates (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule, item 49(a)(ii)):
- **RM1** if the tenancy does not exceed 1 year.
- **RM2** if the tenancy exceeds 1 year but does not exceed 3 years.
- **RM4** if the tenancy exceeds 3 years or has no fixed end date.

The lessee (tenant) is liable to pay the duty on the agreement (Stamp Act 1949, Third Schedule, item 8(a)).

### What could change this
- **Rental amount**: Higher rent increases the amount above RM2,400.
- **Tenancy duration**: Longer terms multiply the rate per RM250.
- **Upfront fees**: Extra duty applies if you pay a premium (an upfront lump-sum payment) (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule, item 49(b)–(c)).
- **Extra copies**: Stamping duplicate copies costs additional fixed duty (Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule, item 41).

*Note: This corpus covers federal principal Acts only. Check lom.agc.gov.my to verify the latest text.*

**Two weeks of notice is less than the statutory minimum, which is at least 4 weeks unless your written contract provides otherwise.**

### What the law says
Under (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)), notice length is set by your written contract of service (employment agreement), or if the contract does not specify a period, it must not be less than:
- 4 weeks if you have been employed for less than 2 years;
- 6 weeks if you have been employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years;
- 8 weeks if you have been employed for 5 years or more.

### What could change this
- **Your written contract**: Notice is set by any written clause in your contract, provided the termination is not due to redundancy (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
- **Redundancy or closure**: If termination is due to business closure, downsizing, or ownership change, the 4 to 8 week minimum applies "regardless of anything to the contrary contained in the contract of service" (Employment Act 1955, s.12(3)).
- **Payment instead of notice**: An employer can terminate earlier by paying an indemnity (wages in place of notice) for the unserved period (Employment Act 1955, s.13(1)).
- **Misconduct**: An employer may dismiss without notice after due inquiry (a proper investigation) for misconduct (Employment Act 1955, s.14(1)).
- **Location**: This Act applies to Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, but not Sabah or Sarawak (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)).

*Note: You can verify the latest consolidated legislation at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**No, an employer cannot dismiss you without a proper reason. If you are dismissed without a valid reason, federal law allows you to challenge the dismissal.**

What the law says
- If you consider that you were dismissed "without just cause or excuse" (without a fair and valid reason), you may make written representations to be reinstated (getting your job back) within 60 days of the dismissal (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.20(1), s.20(1A)).
- For misconduct (wrongdoing or breaking work rules), an employer may dismiss you only "after due inquiry" (a proper internal investigation or hearing) (Employment Act 1955, s.14(1)(a)).
- An employer may end a contract of service (an employment contract) by giving written notice or paying wages in place of notice (Employment Act 1955, s.12(1), s.13(1)).

What could change this
- Which state you work in: the Employment Act 1955 applies only to Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan; Sabah and Sarawak have separate labour ordinances not contained in this federal corpus (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)).
- Genuine redundancy (your job role is no longer needed) or business closure (Employment Act 1955, s.12(3)).
- Specific standards for what constitutes a fair reason depend on Industrial Court case law, which is outside this statutory corpus.

Always verify the current statute text at lom.agc.gov.my.

**You register a trade union by applying to the Director General of Trade Unions within 6 months of forming the union. The application must be signed by at least 7 members and submitted with the union rules, officer details, and the required fee.**

**What the law says**
- An application "shall be signed by at least seven members of the union" using the official form (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.10(1)).
- The application must include the prescribed fee (legally set fee), a printed copy of the union's rules in the national language signed by the applicants, the union's name and head office address, and particulars of the applicants and officers (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.10(2)).
- A union must apply within 6 months of establishment (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.8(1)).
- The Director General (the government official heading the Trade Unions department) may request additional information (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.14) and issues a certificate of registration once registered (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.13).

**What could change this**
- Whether the Director General grants an extension of the application deadline, which cannot exceed 12 months in total (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.8(2)).
- Special membership restrictions, such as rules for public officers (government employees) (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.27(1)) or students (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.26(1)).
- Prescribed application forms and fee amounts are detailed in subsidiary legislation (regulations), not the principal Act.

*Please verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*
